title: ZooKeeper and etcd
description: Compare ZAB protocol and Raft in practice through ZooKeeper and etcd: ephemeral nodes, watches, distributed locks, and Kubernetes control plane.

segments.text: Consensus algorithms are theory. ZooKeeper and etcd are what you actually deploy. They're coordination services: small, strongly consistent key-value stores purpose-built for distributed system metadata. They're not your database. They're the brain that tells your database which node is the leader.

ZooKeeper uses ZAB, ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast. Like Raft, it has a single leader that processes all writes. Followers replicate the leader's log. But ZAB was designed before Raft, and it handles leader election and recovery differently. The key distinction: ZAB guarantees that all messages from a previous leader are delivered before a new leader takes over.

ZooKeeper's killer feature: ephemeral nodes. They exist only as long as the client session is alive. If a service creates an ephemeral node at slash services slash payment dash service dash 1 and that service crashes, the node automatically disappears. Other services watching that path get notified. Instant, reliable service discovery without polling.

Watches are event subscriptions. A client says 'notify me when this path changes.' The next time someone writes to that path, ZooKeeper sends a one-time notification to the watcher. One-time is important: after receiving the event, you must re-register the watch. This prevents the thundering herd that would occur if watches were permanent and thousands of clients watched the same key.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is a one-time watch better than a persistent subscription for a coordination service?

segments.text: The distributed lock recipe using ZooKeeper: create an ephemeral sequential node under a lock path. If your node has the lowest sequence number, you hold the lock. Otherwise, watch the next-lowest node and wait. When that node disappears, check again. If the lock holder crashes, its ephemeral node vanishes, and the next waiter acquires the lock automatically.

etcd is the modern alternative, built on Raft. It uses a flat key-value model instead of ZooKeeper's hierarchical tree. The API is gRPC with protocol buffers. It supports range queries, transactions with compare-and-swap, and lease-based TTLs, which are etcd's version of ephemeral nodes. Most importantly, it's the backend of every Kubernetes cluster.

In Kubernetes, etcd stores everything: pod definitions, service endpoints, config maps, secrets. The API server is the only component that talks to etcd directly. When you run kubectl apply, the API server writes to etcd, and watchers on those keys trigger the scheduler, controller manager, and kubelets to act. etcd is literally the source of truth for your entire cluster.

ZooKeeper versus etcd: ZooKeeper has a richer data model with hierarchy and ephemeral nodes. etcd has simpler operations but better performance, doing thousands of writes per second on SSDs. ZooKeeper is Java, etcd is Go. ZooKeeper requires external client libraries, etcd has a built-in HTTP API. Both are production-proven at massive scale.
segments.thought_prompt: If you were starting a new project today, would you choose ZooKeeper or etcd? What factors matter?

segments.text: Common mistakes with coordination services. First: using them as a general-purpose database. They're designed for small metadata, not large datasets. etcd recommends under 8 GB total. Second: not monitoring leader elections. Frequent elections indicate network instability. Third: storing secrets in ZooKeeper without encryption; it's not a secrets manager.

ZooKeeper and etcd are the unsung heroes of distributed infrastructure. They're small, quiet services that most developers never interact with directly. But when they go down, everything goes down. Understand them, respect them, and monitor them relentlessly. Your entire platform depends on their three-node or five-node cluster staying healthy.
